claims.text: The starting material is nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11.
The intervention changes the composition to approximately W38Ta36Cr11V15 by replacing 4 at.% chromium with vanadium.
Increasing vanadium to about 15 at.% will inhibit radiation-induced precipitation at approximately 8 dpa.
The compositional change will not increase irradiation hardening.
The compositional change will improve suitability for practical bulk fabrication.
Krypton-ion irradiation is an appropriate energetic-particle surrogate for fusion-relevant irradiation.
Increasing vanadium will modify solute segregation at grain boundaries and irradiation-induced point-defect clusters.
Additional vanadium will preferentially segregate to radiation-induced defect sites.
Vanadium segregation to radiation-induced defect sites will retard precipitate nucleation and growth.
The modified defect chemistry will maintain a microstructure resistant to additional hardening.
At approximately 8 dpa, the modified alloy may have about 50% lower radiation-induced precipitate volume fraction than the unmodified alloy.
Irradiation hardening in the modified alloy will remain negligible or only slightly elevated relative to the unmodified alloy.
Reduced precipitation and limited hardening will improve processing characteristics for bulk fabrication.
Unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 typically precipitates under irradiation.
Unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 exhibits negligible irradiation hardening.
The proposed grain-boundary-mediated effects remain operative at service temperatures below those causing extensive thermal recrystallization.
A failure to achieve at least about 50% lower precipitate volume fraction, or an increase in hardening beyond the negligible baseline change, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis says the intervention will not increase irradiation hardening, whereas the predicted outcome permits slightly elevated hardening.
